cards.text: The Song of Songs is a love poem between a young woman and the man she calls “my beloved” (Song of Solomon 2:16). Now voices call out to her, the Shulammite: “Come back, come back,” and then they say it AGAIN. Four “come backs,” friend, and I've had alarm clocks with less commitment than that.

cards.question: The voices want the Shulammite to come back so they can gaze upon her.

cards.text: Then comes a question: “Why do you look at the Shulammite, as on the dance of Mahanaim?” Back when her beloved first described her, he started up top with her eyes (Song of Solomon 4:1), but this time the description takes the scenic route.

cards.question: This time, the description of the Shulammite starts at her feet and works its way up to her head.

cards.text: Up it climbs, from her sandaled feet to her waist to her neck “like a tower made of ivory” and her eyes like the pools of Heshbon. Meanwhile, the nicest thing anybody ever said to ME was my oven timer going BEEP, and even that was just to tell me I burned the batch.

cards.question: At the top, the speaker says the Shulammite's hair is like purple threads, and “the king is captured in your tresses.” What is that picture saying?

answers.text: The king can't take his eyes off her
The king has been taken as a prisoner
The king is hiding from his enemies

cards.text: Then the speaker steps back and takes it all in: “How fair and pleasant you are, O love, with your delights!” Her stature, the speaker says, is like a palm tree, and friend, the closest I ever got to that was somebody calling me “short and sturdy.”

cards.question: The speaker has just compared the Shulammite to a palm tree, and now says, “I will climb the palm tree; I will take hold of its fruit.” What is that picture showing?

answers.text: The speaker longs to be close to her
The speaker wants to gather a harvest
The speaker plans to guard her from others

cards.text: Next come wishes, breath like apples and a mouth like the finest wine, and then the line turns: “May it flow smoothly to my beloved, gliding gently over lips and teeth.” Friend, I've been dropped, scraped and shoved in a drawer, and NOTHING about me has ever glided gently.

cards.question: Then the Shulammite speaks up with one short line about who she belongs to. What does she say?

answers.text: She belongs to her beloved and he desires her
She belongs to her mother and must obey her
She belongs to her family and must stay home

cards.question: Right after that, the Shulammite invites her beloved to the countryside to spend the night among the wildflowers.

cards.text: And after that, she wants them off to the vineyards, and not just any time, but EARLY. Friend, some of us need a whole batch of cookies before we can even SAY the word “early.”

cards.question: In the vineyards, the Shulammite wants to see if the vine has ___ and if the pomegranates are in bloom.

cards.text: And there, she says, she'll give him her love. Even the mandrakes are sending out their fragrance, and friend, when the PLANTS are wearing perfume, you know it's a big day.

cards.question: The Shulammite says that at their door is every delicacy, new as well as old. Who has she treasured them up for?

cards.text: Then she makes a wish: “O that you were to me like a brother who nursed at my mother’s breasts!” Before anybody's eyebrows go up as high as mine, stay with me, friend, because she tells us exactly WHY.

cards.question: Why does the Shulammite wish her beloved were like a brother to her?

answers.text: So she could kiss him outdoors and not be despised
So they could share the family vineyard together
So they could inherit their father's land together

cards.question: The Shulammite says she would lead her beloved to the house of her ___, who taught her, and give him spiced wine to drink.

cards.text: Then comes a line we've heard before (Song of Solomon 2:6): “His left hand is under my head, and his right arm embraces me.” And she ends with a charge she's given twice before (Song of Solomon 2:7; 3:5), and friend, when something gets said THREE times, that's not a suggestion: “O daughters of Jerusalem, I adjure you: Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right.”
